Test for an AI product: if you remove the AI and it still works the same, it's not an AI product. Recommendation engines, fraud detection and generative assistants are AI products; a bolted-on chatbot is just an AI feature.

Versus traditional PM: the same core (vision, discovery, MVPs, GTM), plus owning a data strategy, managing behavior that shifts after release, tracking model metrics alongside product metrics, and handling fairness and explainability.

Three types: the AI-powered PM (uses AI tools to work faster), the applied/AI-enabled PM (integrates pre-trained models and LLM APIs into products) and the core/platform AI PM (builds foundation models or ML platforms, needs deep ML knowledge).
AI PMs balance product metrics against model performance, risk and responsible-AI guardrails across an AI-specific lifecycle.
w5d1r2: Most of what an AI PM needs, a good PM already has. AI-first PM adds a thin but important layer of new skills.
The 6 core competencies: 1) AI/ML fundamentals, 2) data literacy and data readiness, 3) prompt craft and AI tool fluency.
4) Working effectively with ML engineers and data scientists, 5) responsible AI and ethical judgment, 6) strategic judgment that AI can't replace.
Employers look for hands-on experience shipping AI features, not just a title change. A common mistake is adding 'AI' to your title without the substance.
Coding isn't required, but you need enough technical fluency to discuss trade-offs credibly.
w5d1r3: In 2023 Netflix offered up to $900,000 for an AI product manager, showing how much companies value the role. The fundamentals (solve real customer problems, own the product lifecycle) stay the same, but the process changes.

Lifecycle: traditional features are deterministic, but AI work is data-driven and experimental. Accessing and cleaning data can take months, models are trained and tuned iteratively (frameworks like CRISP-DM), and the work continues after launch as new data arrives.
Timelines are less predictable. AI PMs set progress milestones instead of fixed delivery dates and plan fallbacks in case the ML approach doesn't meet the bar.
Stakeholders widen: data scientists, data engineers and ML engineers daily, plus legal, compliance and privacy teams. The PM also manages executive hype by explaining what the model can and can't do.

Experimentation and evaluation: treat each model version like an A/B test, design fail-safes, and track model metrics (accuracy, precision, recall, AUC) alongside product metrics, accepting trade-offs between accuracy, speed and cost.
w5d1r4: A roadmap from Aishwarya Srinivasan (ex-Microsoft, Google and IBM data scientist). Most aspiring AI PMs go about it backwards, collecting certificates without shipping anything.
Step 1: learn practical AI basics: models, training vs inference, fine-tuning vs prompting, vector databases and RAG, and latency trade-offs. Enough vocabulary to earn engineers' trust.

Step 2: deconstruct AI products deliberately, one per week (try to break them, guess their system prompts). Step 3: build and ship a tiny AI product, e.g. a resume or cover-letter assistant. You learn that prompts are brittle, latency matters and users behave unexpectedly.

Step 4: understand AI infrastructure as a PM: evals ('what does good look like?'), cost and latency trade-offs (bigger models can cost 3× and respond 2× slower), observability and a practical responsible-AI framework.
Step 5: get visible. Share your work publicly, network and apply. AI PMs now own the full feedback loop, including evals, and agentic AI has raised the bar.
w5d1r5: AI vs ML vs LLM: AI is the umbrella (systems that reason and act), ML learns patterns from data without explicit rules, and LLMs (GPT, Claude) are ML models trained on huge text datasets to predict the next token.

Prompt engineering: the same model gives very different output for 'summarize this report' vs 'summarize in 3 bullets for a CEO with 30 seconds'. AI PMs build prompt systems (structured templates), not one-off magic prompts.
AI agents and workflows: systems that decide and take multi-step actions. Fine-tuning: further training a model on your data for a specialized task or style.

RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) lets models pull fresh or private data (docs, wikis, databases) to ground answers. Hallucination is confident but false output. Guardrails and safety constrain what the model can say or do.
MCP (Model Context Protocol) is like 'Bluetooth for AI', plugging models into tools such as CRMs and email. Evals measure how well your AI actually performs and are essential before and after launch.
w5d1r6: An AI PM sits between AI engineers (who write the code, wire models and run production systems) and the business, deciding what's worth building. The core skills are data literacy and judgment, not coding.
The job has grown: AI features moved from 'a text box calling an API' to agents that browse, write and run code, and coordinate tools, so PMs now design how whole systems behave.
Demand is real. AI PM hiring roughly doubled, and roles asking for AI skills pay about 28% more. Openings currently outnumber qualified candidates.

Key responsibilities: data (where it comes from, how it's labeled, since bad data is usually the real problem), guardrails (what the AI does when unsure: answer, abstain or hand off to a human; which tasks can run autonomously) and defining 'good enough' with evals.
Prepare for today's role, not the one from 3 years ago: build hands-on experience with real AI products and agents.
w5d1r7: A 10-year follow-up to the popular 'Art of Product Management' Wharton lecture: how AI changes each part of the PM role.
Customer insight: AI now synthesizes raw feedback into themes (beyond sentiment analysis and tag clouds), often spotting patterns humans miss.
Analytics: AI writes and runs SQL, analyzes CSVs and Excel files, and visualizes results, connecting directly to data warehouses through MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers.

Ideation and prototyping: AI prototyping lets PMs and designers build working concepts quickly (e.g. Duolingo's chess course came from an enterprising PM–designer duo). Execution: AI speeds up communication such as status updates and stakeholder alignment.
What AI can't replace is taste: non-consensus strategy, a compelling vision and judgment. Taste has never mattered more.
w5d1r8: Google AI Essentials is a free-to-audit, self-paced online course from Google experts (through Grow with Google and Coursera) that teaches AI fundamentals and productive use of AI tools. No experience needed.
Five modules: Introduction to AI, Maximize Productivity With AI Tools, Discover the Art of Prompting, Use AI Responsibly, and Stay Ahead of the AI Curve.
Focus on practical skills: using generative AI for everyday work tasks, writing effective prompts, and recognizing bias and limitations.
Completion earns a Google certificate you can share with employers. It's a good foundation before deeper AI PM material.
w5d1r9: OpenAI Academy is OpenAI's free learning hub for building practical AI skills for work and careers.
Learning paths: core prompting and output-review habits, repeatable AI workflows, and directing work with agents.
Technical tracks: using Codex across the software development lifecycle and building with the OpenAI API.
Strategy track: turning a real AI initiative into a roadmap and an initial AI strategy draft, which is directly useful for AI PMs. There's also content for education and career preparation.
w5d2r1: ML turns data into knowledge through self-learning. Andrew Ng: 'AI is the new electricity'. PMs must speak engineers' language and understand ML's capabilities and limits.

Types: supervised learning (labeled data; classification like spam filters, regression like predicting house prices), unsupervised learning (finding structure, e.g. clustering) and reinforcement learning (learning by maximizing rewards). Supervised learning drives most economic value today.
Neural networks learn through forward propagation (predict), a cost function (measure error), and backpropagation with gradient descent (adjust weights), repeated many times.

Underfitting (high bias) means the model is too simple to fit the data. Overfitting (high variance) means it memorizes training data and fails on new data. Diagnose by comparing training and dev/test error to human-level error.
Split data into training, dev and test sets. Fixes: bigger models or more training for bias, more data or regularization for variance.
w5d2r2: Non-technical PMs need AI/ML fundamentals to build and manage AI products effectively.
AI is the broad goal of machines performing intelligent tasks. ML is the subset where systems learn from data instead of explicit rules.
Key components: data (collected, cleaned, preprocessed), algorithms (learning procedures), models (the trained result), training, and evaluation on unseen data.
Best practices: define the problem and business objective clearly, manage data quality, choose suitable tools (TensorFlow, PyTorch, scikit-learn), and build a multidisciplinary team.
Develop iteratively: start with an MVP, test, gather feedback and improve, and consider ethics and bias throughout.
w5d2r3: The first course of Duke University's AI Product Management Specialization on Coursera: a non-coding introduction to machine learning for PMs.
Covers how ML works and its types, the model development process, and the intuition behind common ML and deep learning algorithms.
Learn the challenges of modeling and how to overcome them, plus best practices for evaluating and interpreting ML models.
Six modules, ending with a hands-on project where you train and optimize a model on a simple real-world problem.
Goal: collaborate confidently with data scientists and engineers and make informed AI product decisions.
w5d2r4: An LLM is essentially two files: a huge parameters file (e.g. Llama 2 70B is about 140GB) and a small program that runs it. Pretraining compresses a large chunk of the internet (about 10TB of text, thousands of GPUs, millions of dollars) into those weights.
The core task is next-word prediction, which forces the model to learn a lot about the world. The knowledge is lossy and 'dreamed', which is why models hallucinate.
Base model → assistant: fine-tune on high-quality Q&A conversations written by human labelers, then refine with human feedback (RLHF).

Capabilities scale predictably with model size and data (scaling laws). Modern LLMs use tools (browsing, calculator, code), are multimodal, and are moving toward slower 'System 2' reasoning and self-improvement. Karpathy frames the LLM as the kernel of a new operating system.
Security challenges: jailbreaks, prompt injection (hidden instructions in web pages or images) and data poisoning/backdoors.
w5d2r5: Pretraining: download and filter web text (e.g. FineWeb), tokenize it into about 100K token types, and train a transformer to predict the next token. The result is a 'base model', an internet document simulator.
Post-training (supervised fine-tuning) on curated conversations turns a base model into a helpful assistant. You're effectively talking to a statistical simulation of an expert labeler.

LLM psychology: hallucinations (mitigated by teaching models to say 'I don't know' and by tools like search), knowledge in weights is a vague memory while the context window is working memory, and models need tokens to think, so step-by-step reasoning helps.
Tokenization quirks explain failures at counting letters or spelling. Intelligence is 'jagged': brilliant at hard tasks, sometimes failing simple ones.
Reinforcement learning lets models discover reasoning strategies ('thinking' models like DeepSeek-R1, much like AlphaGo's move 37). RLHF helps with unverifiable tasks but can be gamed.
w5d2r6: GPT = Generative Pre-trained Transformer. It generates text by repeatedly predicting a probability distribution over the next token, sampling one, appending it, and repeating.
Text is split into tokens, and each token becomes a vector (embedding). Directions in embedding space encode meaning (e.g. king − man + woman ≈ queen).
Inside a transformer, attention blocks let vectors share context with each other, and MLP blocks process each vector. Repeating these layers refines meaning.
Deep learning premise: all behavior comes from tunable weights (GPT-3 has about 175B) organized in matrices, learned from data rather than hand-coded.
At the end, unembedding turns the final vector into scores for every token, and softmax with temperature converts them into probabilities (higher temperature means more random, creative output).
w5d2r7: Attention lets each token's embedding update based on context. 'Mole' means different things in 'American shrew mole', 'one mole of CO2' and 'take a biopsy of the mole'.
Each token produces a query ('what am I looking for?') and a key ('what do I contain?'). Query–key dot products measure relevance, and softmax normalizes them into an attention pattern.
Masking stops tokens from seeing future tokens during training, which is what lets the model predict the next word.
Value vectors carry the information that gets added to relevant embeddings, e.g. adjectives refining the nouns they describe.
Multi-headed attention runs many attention heads in parallel (96 per layer in GPT-3), each learning different relationships. Attention cost grows with the square of context length.
w5d2r8: HelloPM's free AI product management course: 9 masterclasses (12+ hours) across AI PM, core PM skills and career growth.

AI track: how LLMs work (tokens, transformers), the GenAI value stack, RAG (chunking, embeddings, vector DBs), prompt engineering, fine-tuning (full vs PEFT/LoRA) and AI agents (workflow vs autonomous).
Includes product teardowns of Granola, NotebookLM and Lovable, plus AI evals: success criteria, evaluation datasets, LLM-as-judge and continuous monitoring.
Key ideas: context engineering (prompt → RAG → fine-tune) as an AI PM's decision tree, most agent failures come from poor problem definition, and a great AI PM is 'PM first, AI second'.
Other modules cover PRDs, analytics, APIs, PM interviews and salary negotiation.
w5d2r9: Learn Prompting is a large, free, open prompt engineering resource (60+ modules, 9 languages) backed by published research.
Courses include Introduction to Prompt Engineering, LLMs, RAG, Generative AI Agents and practical GenAI for everyday efficiency and marketing.
Also covers AI security: a free 7-day LLM security course (prompt hacking types, common attacks and defenses) and an AI red-teaming masterclass with Sander Schulhoff.
Useful for AI PMs to build practical prompting skills and understand prompt injection and other risks in AI products.
w5d3r1: By Aman Khan (Arize AI, ex-Spotify and Apple) on Lenny's Newsletter: evals, not prompts, are the hidden lever behind great AI products, and writing them is becoming the defining AI PM skill.

Evals break an AI system into steps and measure the impact of each change, replacing 'vibe checks' with data. Running example: a trip-planning agent ('relaxing weekend near SF under $1,000') that uses flight, hotel and map tools.
Human evals: thumbs up/down or expert labelers. Real signal, but sparse, ambiguous and costly.

Code-based evals: deterministic checks (is the API call or code valid? does it run?). LLM-as-judge evals: a judge model grades outputs against a rubric. Scalable, natural-language, and can explain its judgments.
Workflow: define what 'good' means for each step, build a labeled dataset, write eval prompts, check judges against human labels, and iterate continuously as the product changes.
w5d3r2: AI systems are non-deterministic, so you can't manually test your way to confidence. Evals turn 'I think it's better' into 'we tested 200 cases and accuracy rose 5% without hurting tone'.
Evals give PMs coverage (hundreds of scenarios), trade-off visibility and version comparison. Defining 'good' is a product decision, not just an engineering one.

Three components: a dataset (golden cases, edge cases and known failures; start with 5–10 and grow to a golden set), the task (the prompt, chain or agent being tested) and scorers (0–1 scores, one quality dimension each, via code checks or LLM judges).
PMs own success criteria and rubrics, essentially a PRD for AI behavior. Engineers build scorers and infrastructure.
Three phases of agent development lead to automated evaluation and a continuous loop: find issues in production → update datasets and scorers → run evals → improve → monitor.
w5d3r3: AI agents break traditional analytics. Inputs are open-ended chat and outputs are non-deterministic, so click-based tracking can't see what happened inside.
A trace records an entire agent interaction: user input and intent, each tool call (span) and its result, retrieved context (RAG), the final outcome and feedback signals.

Single-trace inspection debugs specific failures (e.g. 'charged twice' traced to a billing tool returning a duplicate row). Aggregate trace analysis finds patterns: failing intents, erroring tools, costly queries.
Evals measure agent quality systematically and connect it to engagement and business outcomes.
PMs who treat eval design as part of the job own the loop between agent quality and business results. Otherwise you ship features you can't measure, debug or defend.
w5d4r1: PMs rarely own the model, but they own the experience and launch criteria, so responsible AI is part of the job. It splits into four areas: bias, fairness, transparency and hallucinations.

Bias: ask which users are missing from the data and who pays when the model errs. Segment model error rates like funnel metrics (a 10-point accuracy gap for one group is a defect), but don't over-correct into failing everyone equally.
Fairness: pick one product-specific definition (e.g. equal approval rates for qualified applicants) and write it in the spec. Run a pre-launch audit on about 1,000 real inputs bucketed by segment.
Transparency: label AI outputs, show confidence for high-stakes answers, let users dispute results, and review disputes regularly.

Hallucinations: sort use cases by blast radius. Low-risk features get light review; high-risk ones need grounding, a human in the loop or checker models. Build escape hatches (retry, fallback to human support).
w5d4r2: PMs decide what AI features ship and how they behave, so responsible AI is a core product responsibility, not just an engineering or legal one.
Key principles: fairness (avoid biased outcomes for user groups), transparency and explainability (users know when AI is involved and why), privacy and data protection, and accountability.
Build responsibility in from discovery: question training data sources, consider who could be harmed, and define acceptable risk before building.
Put guardrails and human oversight in place for high-stakes decisions, and monitor models after launch for drift, bias and misuse.
Balance innovation with trust. Responsible products protect users and the company's reputation long term.
w5d4r3: AI hallucinations are confident but false outputs. In customer experience they damage trust and can scale across thousands of interactions.
Core causes: incomplete, outdated or biased training data (the model fills gaps with assumptions), ambiguous prompts and intent confusion, and a lack of governance and guardrails.
The model isn't lying. It predicts likely patterns, and with an incomplete picture the prediction may not match reality or intent.
Prevention by design: ground AI in unified, real-time data (fewer fragmented bolt-on tools), build in governance and guardrails, and monitor outputs.
Human oversight: human-in-the-loop review, escalation to human agents when requests exceed the AI's limits, and transparency, which matter all the more as agentic AI takes actions.
w5d5r1: A list of 25 common AI PM interview questions with sample answers, from basics to scenarios.
Concepts: how AI products differ from traditional ones, model bias, the cold-start problem, explainability, hallucinations, and A/B testing for AI.
Metrics and evaluation: measuring AI product success, chatbot metrics, and evaluating generative AI products.
Design and scenarios: improve a recommendation system, design a chatbot, improve search with AI, launch a low-accuracy product, debug an AI product.
Collaboration and risk: the PM's role in an AI team, working with data scientists, prioritizing AI features, and handling data privacy.
w5d5r2: 50+ AI PM interview questions with expert answers, grouped by type. AI PM interviews add technical AI depth on top of classic PM rounds.
Technical: supervised vs unsupervised vs reinforcement learning, precision vs recall (and when to optimize each), how LLMs work, RAG vs fine-tuning, and model evaluation metrics.

Product sense and strategy: improve Google Search with AI, design an AI feature for a daily-use product, decide whether every product needs AI, prioritize an AI roadmap with limited ML resources, respond to a competitor's AI launch.
Execution and ethics: diagnose a chatbot getting negative feedback, design AI content moderation, fix a biased recommender.
Behavioral and craft: decisions with incomplete data, disagreeing with engineers, failed launches, staying current, writing PRDs for AI features, and working with ML engineers.
w5d5r3: PM case interviews give a realistic problem (improve an app, diagnose a metric drop, launch a feature). Interviewers judge structure, data use, prioritization and communication over a single 'right' answer.

Steps: clarify the business goal → identify the main user problem → state assumptions → brainstorm → prioritize → recommend an MVP → summarize. CSPMS shorthand: Clarify, Segment, Problem, Metrics, Solution.

25 example cases cover growth (Spotify podcasts, LinkedIn engagement), metric drops (Amazon checkout down 12%, Netflix retention), design (grocery app for seniors), monetization (Duolingo revenue), roadmaps, AI products and trust/security (Airbnb, banking).
Tips: pick one target segment, one primary metric plus 2–3 guardrails, and one realistic MVP, and say what you won't build.
Use AI only when it clearly beats a non-AI solution, and define fallbacks, accuracy and safety. In a 30-minute case, budget time and stay calm when challenged.
w5d5r4: Written by a recruiting firm co-founder, so read it with that bias in mind. AI PM interviews test four signals: AI product sense, evaluating a model that's sometimes wrong, partnering with data science across the model lifecycle, and shipping responsibly under uncertainty.

Cautionary story: a polished candidate aced product sense but froze on evals. She couldn't separate an offline regression set from online metrics and had no fallback plan. The rougher candidate who answered well got the job.

Strong answer pattern: a hand-labeled golden dataset with domain experts, a hallucination-rate threshold you won't ship above, shadow deployment against the current system, and human review below a confidence cutoff.
The job is shipping products built on a component that is probabilistic, sometimes wrong, expensive to run and changing every few months.
The questions come with grading notes on which answers pass and which quietly fail, covering metrics, model lifecycle collaboration and responsible-AI guardrails.
live-session-1: Masterclass by Niranjal Suresh Kumar (IITG and IIM Bangalore alum, PM on Microsoft Copilot agents) on breaking into PM in the AI era.
A PM blends business, technology and UX: understand the user, then craft flows that move them seamlessly toward their goal while balancing user fatigue against business goals.
Role definition: the strategic owner of a product's vision and lifecycle, and the 'single-threaded' owner who aligns multiple teams. When something goes wrong, people come to you.

Breaking in: be a PM of your own career. Build original products, prototype quickly with AI tools, enter case competitions, share your work publicly, and build a strong community and referral network.
Communication is the biggest lever: storytelling, positioning and concise answers (practise answering in under 50 words).
live-session-2: Session by Anil Kumar Shahi (IIT Roorkee and IIM Ahmedabad alum, PM at Tata 1mg) on building product sense.

Product sense combines user psychology, critical reasoning, prioritization, UX sensibility, data fluency and tech awareness. Understanding user psychology is the most unique and important part, and it takes practice.
Example: why Instagram Stories works (borrowed from Snapchat). Ephemeral, low-pressure sharing visible for 24 hours.
Persona creation: there are endless ways to slice users. Better segmentation follows the user lifecycle, e.g. Instamart new vs repeat users, then by acquisition channel and behavior.
Knowing exactly who you're solving for leads you to the right problems, and good solutions follow from the right problem statements.
live-session-3: Session by Akhil, founder of Product Space, on understanding users and UI/UX, which he calls the toughest part of PM.

User segmentation: group users into cohorts by shared characteristics, which is everywhere in daily life. Top-of-mind awareness decides which apps users go to first (e.g. Flipkart and Amazon for online shopping).
Market context matters: early Indian e-commerce (2012–15) was immature, with room for several players (Flipkart, Amazon, Jabong, Snapdeal) to become category creators by winning users fast.
UX goal: a frictionless interface that lets users complete the goal they came for (e.g. ordering food on Swiggy from a well-structured homepage with search and recommendations).
Shows how AI design tools can fast-track product design beyond traditional tools like Figma.
live-session-4: Session on measuring success, from metrics to product-market fit.
Metric focus shifts across the product life cycle: acquisition in introduction, engagement and retention in growth, monetization in maturity, and sunset or spin-off decisions in decline.
Product-market fit sits within this: the alignment of a product's features with the target market's needs.
Measuring the wrong metric is disastrous. The US in Vietnam optimized for kill ratio, 'won' on it and still lost the war. Pick outcome-based metrics.
Metric trees: break a north star such as listening time into levers like more users (notifications, trending artists, recommendations) × time per session (playlists, personalization).
live-session-5: Session by a Dream11 PM on MVP and GTM: building and launching products.
India is now the world's third-largest startup hub (about 150K startups a year), and AI is making building even faster.

MVPs evolve with user feedback (e.g. Swiggy's journey from food delivery toward Instamart and more). The MVP phase never ends, because new features start as MVPs. Skip the MVP route only when strong evidence exists (Blinkit scaling after seeing Instamart's traction).
'If a picture is worth a thousand words, a prototype is worth a thousand meetings.' Tools like Lovable let PMs test many ideas cheaply, knowing most will fail.
GTM alignment: product, marketing and sales must share the same understanding of the problem, user, pricing and positioning. Promising one thing in an ad and showing another on landing breaks trust.
live-session-6: Session by Product Space on AI tools for PMs and preparing for AI PM interviews.
AI won't replace PMs. Products are end-to-end workflows that need judgment and direction, and that judgment is what differentiates one company from another when everyone has access to the same LLMs.
Expectations are rising: PMs now need to understand classical ML (regression, decision trees, boosting), generative AI (LLMs, SLMs) and agentic AI, and the field moves fast, so keep upskilling.
Stay updated with real industry practice (e.g. how teams build AI recommendation engines) by learning the fundamentals first.
Interviews: classic product sense, execution and strategy questions remain, plus subject-matter AI questions. Avoid over-relying on ChatGPT for your thinking.
live-session-7: A 90-minute Product Space masterclass on tech basics for PMs, with hands-on API practice.

How the internet works: a web address (URL) is like a house address. HTTPS is the protocol (the way information travels), a domain name is the readable name, and DNS maps it to a numeric IP address, like a phone book.
Databases and SQL: SQL (structured query language) talks to relational databases and powers CRUD operations. How much a PM needs depends on the company and whether dedicated analysts are available.

APIs, hands-on in Postman: endpoints, parameters, authentication vs authorization, and importing a cURL command. Status codes tell teams what went wrong (200 = working, 400 = bad request) so bugs can be diagnosed faster.
E-commerce example: homepage → search → product listing page (PLP) → product detail page (PDP), each step calling an API. Validate inputs up front in the UI (e.g. email format) to reduce failures.
